name: Freya Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm assistant manager for Greenacre Farming, a contract farming company. That means landowners pay us to run their farms for them. We've got five farms around Elmbridge, mostly wheat, barley and oilseed rape, plus 1,200 ewes. Half my day is out with the sheep or on a tractor, and half is in the pickup on my phone, doing the staff rota, ordering seed and fertiliser and keeping spray records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, and I like being trusted. What wears me out is being the person everyone rings. If a ewe's stuck or a delivery's late, it's my phone. I use an AI app now and then to tidy the spray records, which helps, but I don't trust it with the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, that's a relief for planning purposes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I'd probably say it in the office at Elmbridge with a bit of a grin, because some of the lads were sure robots would be driving the combines by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a good spot. My job's steady, Sam's busy as an electrician, and we've got about five months saved. The only thing on my mind is that we want to buy a house and prices in Elmbridge keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job. Keep using the AI app for records, maybe a bit more for the rota. Sam and I would go ahead with buying a two-bed in 2027 like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house plan, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're looking at a two-bed on Station Road, around 190,000. We've got most of a deposit. If nothing big changes, we'd buy next autumn after harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the routine AI stuff change anything in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in a good way. The spray records take me twenty minutes instead of an hour, and that's an hour I get back on a Friday.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, with a grin in the Elmbridge office.
I'd tease colleagues who thought **robots** would drive the combines.
think: I'm in a **good spot** with a steady job and five months saved.
My only real pressure is **house prices** in Elmbridge rising.
do: Keep the **same job** and use the AI app for records and rota.
Buy a **two-bed** on Station Road next autumn after harvest.
S0.quote: The spray records take me twenty minutes instead of an hour, and that's an hour I get back on a Friday.
fieldNote: Her household is **secure**: steady job, busy partner, five months saved.
AI's small gain is **time back**, which she values.
Her only real pressure is **housing costs**.

steps.text: Keep running sheep, tractors and staff rotas for Greenacre
Buy the two-bed on Station Road next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Now that one does touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to adapt and be sensible about it. Farming has always changed. I'd say it at work like it's no big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, half of my job is on that card. Rotas, ordering, records, planning, that's the half that pays me more than a farm worker. If software does it, Greenacre might have one assistant manager covering ten farms instead of two of us covering five each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the farm management software Greenacre already pays for, so I'm the one running it, not replaced by it. I'd hold off the house purchase by six months and keep the savings up. And I'd ask my boss, Martin, directly what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd notice it every time I opened the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Martin directly. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Martin if Greenacre plans to cut assistant manager jobs in the next two years. Martin's straight with me, so I'd get a straight answer, even if it's a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Craig, the other assistant manager. Craig's 45 and hates computers. If Greenacre (the farming company she works for) picks between me and Craig (the other assistant manager), it'd be me who stays, and I'd feel guilty about that.

I'd talk about it at work like it's **no big deal**.
think: **Half my job** is on that card: rotas, ordering, records and planning.
Greenacre might keep **one assistant manager** instead of two.

fieldNote: Her role is more **desk-heavy** than a typical farm worker's, so she feels it now.

Her calm **public face** hides a sharper private worry.

steps.text: Learn the farm management software until she runs it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard and we'll all need help. I'd keep it practical in public, talking about training and support, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk half goes in 2028, and the field half goes around 2031. So I'd likely be out of a manager's job by 2028 and out of farming by 2031. Sam's the safer one, because somebody has to wire up all those robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the house purchase for now and keep the deposit as savings, around 30,000. I'd talk to Sam about joining his electrical business, doing farm robot installs, and start an electrician's course at the college in Wexley in 2027. I'd keep working at Greenacre as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground had moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd lose the better-paid half of my job first, then keep sheep and tractors for three years on a farm worker's pay. That's maybe 6,000 less a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sam react to you joining his business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say yes straight away, then worry about it at night. Sam's always wanted a business partner, but not like this, out of panic.

fieldNote: The **three-year gap** splits her income loss into two steps.

Sam's **electrical trade** becomes the household lifeline.

steps.text: Drop the house purchase and keep the 30,000 deposit as savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's more workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people start now. I'd tell my colleagues to pick up new skills while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with five years I could move into the robot side of farming before the desk work goes. By 2031 I'd want to be the person who sets up and checks the machines, not the one doing rotas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the agricultural robotics certificate at the Wexley college next year, part-time. I'd use the AI tools for everything at work now, to get fluent. Sam and I would buy a cheaper house, a 160,000 one, in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a cheaper house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know what I'll earn in 2032. A smaller mortgage means I could take a pay cut and still sleep. Sam agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Craig to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, gently. Craig's got kids and a mortgage, so his five years feels shorter than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like normal life with a big change at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a long runway, and it's on all of us to use it. Nobody gets to say they weren't warned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be 37 by 2036 and 40 by 2039, with plenty of time to move into robot work or management of machines. The bigger question is whether Greenacre still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the Station Road house as planned in 2027. I'd learn the AI tools steadily, once the bigger farms prove them. Around 2030 I'd do the robotics certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wonder whether Greenacre exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because contract farming is basically organising people and machines for landowners. If the machines organise themselves, landowners might just rent robots instead of hiring a contract farming company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too much over ten years. I'd see it coming and I'd jump before the company sinks.

say: I'd call ten years a **long runway** that we all must use.
I'd say **nobody** gets to claim they weren't warned.
think: I'd be **fine**, with time to move into robot work by 40.
The bigger question is whether **Greenacre** survives as a company.
do: Buy the **Station Road** house as planned in 2027.
Learn AI tools steadily once **bigger farms** prove them.
S4.quote: If the machines organise themselves, landowners might just rent robots instead of hiring a contract farming company.
fieldNote: With a decade, her worry moves from her **role** to her **employer**.
She would wait for **proof** before adopting, true to her steady style.
Her house plan goes ahead **on schedule**.

steps.text: Buy the Station Road house in 2027 as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the desk half of my job straight away and the rest three years later. What would help is cheap, fast training courses for farm staff, run near us, not in some city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the staff. Everyone thinks of farmers as owners, but loads of us are staff, and nobody plans for the staff.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks of farmers as owners, but loads of us are staff, and nobody plans for the staff.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old **assistant manager** at a contract farming company.
Half her day is **desk work**, so Steady Disruption hits her early.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once they're proven.
She is **calm** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
Her partner Sam's **electrical trade** is her fallback and possible new career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing the desk half of her job immediately.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, fast training** for farm staff, run locally rather than in cities.
